subject: english-literature
title: Contextual Lenses
welcome_lead: Texts speak across centuries. Use historical, social and critical contexts to power your comparison.
meta_desc: Contextual lenses for comparative study at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have framed two texts in their contexts and let the contexts speak to one another through the texts.

concepts.def: The social and political moment of a text's production — Restoration, Romantic, Modernist.
Class, gender, race and economic conditions shaping characters and reception.
How a text was read at the time and since — Leavis on Lawrence, Said on Conrad.
Kristeva's term — every text is a tissue of citations from prior texts.
How later versions (film, stage, novelisation) shape current readings.
Comparing texts from different periods to trace continuity and change.

walkthroughs.body_html: Compare a 17th-century carpe diem lyric with a 21st-century love poem and the contexts of mortality and gender shift the same trope's meaning.
How a text was read shapes how we read. Postcolonial readings (Achebe on Heart of Darkness) reframe a canonical novella as part of the imperial archive.
Comparative study often becomes the search for intertexts — Eliot quoting Dante, Atwood rewriting the Odyssey. Texts speak to texts.

mcqs.q: Why does historical context matter when reading literature?
options: An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
Context just means writing about what the author had for breakfast.
Context is required because all texts are about history.
Texts emerge from and respond to specific historical conditions — context illuminates references, assumptions and arguments that might otherwise be invisible.
Postmodernism means writing about the future.
Postmodernism just means literature written after modernism.
An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
Self-aware metafiction, intertextuality, scepticism toward grand narratives, playfulness with form, and blurring of high/low culture.
An unreliable narrator is one who tells lies in the story.
Postmodernism means writing about the future.
Their account is undermined within the text by ignorance, bias, self-deception or deceit, so the reader must read against what they say.
